items.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: like Coleman Hawkins was a cello player. But he couldn’t get a job in the symphony orchestra.

ctx.x: Have you played in Europe? Tell us about playing outside the United States. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

Well in Europe it’s a different ball game. The people in Europe, well almost all the people that come to a jazz festival or jazz clubs are intellectuals or students. And they feel that this is the only art form that American gave to the world was this music. And so they accept us, in fact, there was a time that they felt that nobody white could play jazz, because everybody black was playing it. There was a time that there were very few white guys that even thought of playing jazz. Because like I say it was a…
Let me ask you, how did you get the nickname “Panama?”

items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: Coleman Hawkins had just come in town from Europe, and we all went over to the Famous Door to see him

ctx.x: few musicians that had played around Miami. So I was sort of shy to go up to the bandstand and introduce myself; and furthermore, there were so many people around the guys in the band, I wouldn't have gotten the chance to speak to them anyway.

But I did get a chance to meet Joe in 1939 at the Famous Door when I was playing with Roy --I had just joined Roy, and Coleman Hawkins had just come in town from Europe, and we all went over to the Famous Door to see him, and that was when I met Joe Jones.
Oh, you never saw him play with the band, then?
